transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-10
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jasper Lin (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Omega Head of ML), Rajiv Menon (Omega Platform), Priya Kapoor (Omega Procurement)

Summary (auto): quick POC scoping focused on cost modeling, workload sizing, and benchmark plan. Customer has tight budget for inference (~$10k/month) and needs to validate latency under 100ms p95 for short chat-like prompts and 3-5s for long-form generation. Discussed batching, KV cache, quantization trade-offs and Dedicated vs Hosted. Agreed next steps: send cost model spreadsheet, run a 48h benchmark, share security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda - align on success criteria for the POC, capture workload sizing, then agree benchmark plan and timelines. Jasper will jump into config details.
[00:12] Lena: sounds good. quick context: we run a customer support assistant and a summarize flow. typical request is ~50 tokens input, ~120 tokens output; but we also have long summarization jobs that are 2k to 4k output tokens. our target is to keep chat p95 under 100 ms for the short path and allow longer latency for long runs. budget wise procurement is pushing for unit cost to average under $0.0006 per token overall, and total monthly spend target is $10k.
[00:39] Jasper: ok, thanks. super helpful. couple clarifying q's - what's your concurrency pattern? is it spiky (user-facing) or steady (background)?
[00:46] Rajiv: mainly spiky during business hours; base concurrency around 30 RPS and spikes to 220 for short bursts. long summarization jobs come in asynchronously maybe 10 per hour.
[00:57] Maya: perfect, so two workloads: user-facing low-latency chat and async long-run summarization. for cost modeling we look at per-token compute, batching gains, and cache hits. one useful rule: batching helps throughput but increases p95. so we'll show both dedicated and hosted numbers.
[01:15] Lena: question - are you expecting us to run on Redwood Dedicated or can we start on Hosted? we need to know security implications and costs.
[01:21] Maya: can do both. Hosted is fastest to start and lower up-front; Dedicated gives more predictable throughput and often lower per-token cost if you commit. also Dedicated simplifies meeting strict latency windows since you control the pool. for SOC2 and KMS we can run Private if required but that's a bigger ops lift.
[01:37] Priya: Procurement note - if this goes to Dedicated which requires an annual commit, we need a clear ROI and a 90 day pilot option.
[01:44] Jasper: noted. on the technical side, for cost estimation we model: tokens per request, average tokens per month, effective tokens after caching, and batching factor. e.g., if you get 30 RPS steady and bursts to 220, average batching across the fleet might be 1.2x for user-facing but 4x-8x for background summarization depending on how we schedule.
[02:05] Lena: can you give a back-of-envelope per-token number? that helps us compare to the $0.0006 target.
[02:10] Jasper: right now with an open model at 16-bit FP on a single GPU and Hosted pricing, raw compute tends to be around $0.0008 to $0.0012 per generated token for medium-sized models (e.g., 7b-13b family) if no batching/caching. With batching you can shave that by 20-50% depending on how well requests line-up. KV cache for repeated prefixes can drop effective generated tokens by 10-30% for chat flows with repetition. So blended, hitting $0.0006 is tight but plausible if you: (a) pick a cost-efficient model (quantized 4-bit or 8-bit), (b) accept some batching, and (c) leverage caching.
[02:48] Rajiv: is quantization supported on Redwood? what's the impact on latency and quality?
[02:52] Jasper: yes, we support quantized variants; typical tradeoffs: 4-bit quantization reduces memory and increases throughput, so per-token cost drops ~30-60%, but you may see slight quality regressions on edge cases. we recommend running sample evals. for latency, quantized runs are often faster per-token, but model kernel characteristics matter - we'll pick the best kernel per hardware.
[03:12] Lena: okay. regarding benchmarks, what exactly will you run for us?
[03:16] Maya: proposed benchmark plan:
 - 48-hour mixed workload run: simulate business-hour spikes and background summarization.
 - Two model variants: quantized 4-bit 13b and fp16 7b as a lower-latency baseline.
 - Measure p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, tokens/sec, and effective cost-per-generated-token after batching and cache.
 - We'll also run quality checks (ROUGE/BLEU or embedding-based similarity) on sampled outputs to ensure degradation isn't material.
[03:44] Rajiv: for the sim we'll provide a 7-day traffic profile. can you simulate our spike pattern?
[03:49] Jasper: yes, we'll replay the traffic with the same arrival pattern and content length distribution. important to include real prompt set because token split matters a lot.
[03:57] Priya: procurement wants to see an example cost calc showing worst-case and optimistic-case monthly spend. can you provide those?
[04:04] Maya: yes - we'll send a spreadsheet with three scenarios: baseline (no batching, hosted fp16), optimized-hosted (batching + caching + quantized where applicable), and dedicated-commit (reserved capacity with 20% discount and higher batching). the sheet will show tokens/month x cost/token = monthly compute cost plus an estimated infra surcharge.
[04:23] Lena: quick nit - how do you model cache hit rate? our chat tends to have a lot of repeated prefixes (greeting + system prompt), but customers are unique per session.
[04:31] Jasper: we model prefix caching at two levels: system/static prompt cache (high hit rates, 40-60%) and session-level KV cache for multi-turn (lower, 10-25% depending on average turns). we'll parameterize those as inputs to the spreadsheet so you can vary them.
[04:45] Rajiv: for our SLOs, p95 < 100ms on short path is hard if batching aggregates 5-10 requests. will you show latency vs batching curves?
[04:54] Jasper: yes, we'll produce plots: p95 latency vs batching factor and throughput. typically for small requests batching factor above ~1.5 starts to push p95 beyond 100ms depending on model and infra. that's why Dedicated is attractive: you can reduce batching by dedicating capacity and still be cost-effective.
[05:11] Lena: what about autoscaling? we can't overprovision constantly.
[05:15] Maya: Dedicated supports autoscaling policies with burst capacity; we can set target utilization to balance cost and latency. as part of the POC we'll suggest policy parameters.
[05:23] Priya: also need to confirm data retention and audit logs for procurement.
[05:27] Maya: we'll attach our SOC2 summary and logging docs. if you need Private deployment for on-prem/KMS, we'll include the scope and rough timeline - that takes longer to stand up (4-8 weeks typically).
[05:39] Lena: timeline question - we want results within three weeks if possible. is that feasible?
[05:43] Jasper: operationally yes:
 - Week 1: agree prompts, traffic profile, and success criteria. provision test env.
 - Week 2: run 48-72h benchmark and initial cost analysis.
 - Week 3: iterate on model/hyperparams and deliver final cost model and recommendation.
So three weeks from kickoff is reasonable.
[06:03] Rajiv: any gotchas we should be aware of? network egress or storage costs?
[06:07] Maya: good point - we'll include an itemized cost line for egress and storage for logs/checkpoints. usually compute dominates but egress can add up for high-volume embeddings.
[06:16] Lena: can you put an example calculation in chat now for baseline numbers? just a quick line.
[06:19] Jasper: sure: assume 2 million generated tokens/day -> 60M tokens/month. at $0.0009/token (hosted fp16, no batching) that's $54k/month. with batching and caching you might get to $0.0005 effective token -> $30k/month. with Dedicated commit and aggressive quantization maybe $0.00035 -> $21k/month. so to hit the $10k target we'd need either much lower token volume or heavier quality/perf tradeoffs or a deeper committed discount.
[06:48] Priya: that helps - procurement sees those ranges.
[06:52] Lena: quality checks - how do you measure degradation from quantization?
[06:56] Jasper: we run side-by-side eval: embedding similarity, exact-match for critical outputs, and human review on a sample. we'll include thresholds you can approve.
[07:06] Maya: ok last part - success criteria recap. what do you need to see to call the POC successful?
[07:11] Lena: we need evidence that: (1) p95 latency for chat path is <=100ms in production-like traffic, (2) monthly cost estimate <= $10k or a clear path with tradeoffs to get there, (3) model quality within X% of our baseline on our eval set, (4) security docs acceptable for procurement.
[07:29] Maya: good. we'll map those to measurable checkpoints and pass/fail thresholds in the spreadsheet.
[07:35] Rajiv: can you confirm what we'll need from us? we heard prompts, traffic profile, access to a small set of live traffic or synthetic generator, and a contact for infra changes.
[07:44] Jasper: plus any SSO/KMS constraints so we pick the right deployment mode.
[07:47] Lena: we'll send prompts and the traffic CSV by Thursday (2025-03-13).
[07:50] Maya: great. thanks everyone. we'll send the cost-model spreadsheet and benchmark plan by Wednesday (2025-03-12) and aim to start the benchmarks as soon as we have the traffic profile.
[07:58] Priya: procurement will review SOC2 and T&Cs - please send docs to procurement@omegasolutions.com.
[08:04] Maya: noted.

End recap (auto):
- Agreed POC scope: 48h mixed-workload benchmark across two model variants, quality checks, and cost modeling.
- Success criteria: p95 chat <= 100ms, monthly cost target <= $10k or clear options to hit it, quality within baseline, procurement signoff on security docs.
- Deliverables: benchmark results, cost model spreadsheet, SOC2/security docs, and recommendation (hosted vs dedicated).
- Owners & due dates: Maya send spreadsheet by 2025-03-12; Jasper prepare benchmark by 2025-03-14; Omega to send prompts and traffic by 2025-03-13.
